subject: Genetics
topic: Robertsonian Translocation Down Syndrome Recurrence Risk
stem: A 28-year-old G1P1 woman and her 30-year-old husband present for genetic counseling following the birth of their first child, who was diagnosed with Down syndrome. Cytogenetic karyotype analysis of the infant confirms an unbalanced Robertsonian translocation involving chromosomes 14 and 21: 46,XY,der(14;21)(q10;q10),+21. High-resolution parental karyotyping demonstrates that the father possesses a normal 46,XY karyotype, whereas the mother is an asymptomatic carrier of a balanced Robertsonian translocation: 45,XX,der(14;21)(q10;q10). The parents plan future childbearing and inquire about the precise risk of having another child with Down syndrome. Which of the following best represents the empirical recurrence risk of Down syndrome in subsequent liveborn children of this couple, and the biological reason for this rate?

options.text: Approximately 10% to 15%; theoretical gametic segregation of 33% is attenuated by high intrauterine lethality of unbalanced conceptions
options.explanation: The mother is a balanced carrier of a Robertsonian der(14;21) translocation. During meiosis I, the translocated chromosome pairs with chromosomes 14 and 21 to form a trivalent structure. Theoretical segregation yields 6 possible gametic types: normal (14, 21), balanced translocation der(14;21), translocated trisomy 21 (der[14;21], 21), monosomy 21 (14), trisomy 14 (der[14;21], 14), and monosomy 14 (21). Monosomies 14 and 21 and trisomy 14 are non-viable, leaving 3 viable theoretical gametic outcomes: normal, balanced carrier, and Down syndrome (theoretical risk 1 in 3, or 33%). However, the EMPIRICAL recurrence risk in liveborn offspring of female balanced der(14;21) carriers is approximately 10% to 15% (and < 2% if the father is the carrier). This marked discrepancy between theoretical (33%) and empirical (10-15%) risk arises because unbalanced trisomy 21 embryos frequently undergo spontaneous first-trimester embryonic resorption and miscarriage.

options.text: Approximately 33%; Mendelian segregation predicts one viable trisomic conceptus for every three surviving zygotes
options.explanation: While 33% is the theoretical Mendelian gametic risk based on the 3 viable gametic outcomes, the observed empirical recurrence rate in liveborns is 10% to 15% because many unbalanced fetuses spontaneously abort.

options.text: Approximately 50%; the translocated derivative chromosome segregates into half of all functional maternal gametes
options.explanation: Robertsonian segregation involves a trivalent complex resulting in 6 possible gametes (3 viable), not a simple 1:1 Mendelian monogenic split.

options.text: Approximately 1% to 2%; post-zygotic meiotic rescue selectively degrades excess chromosomal material in maternal oocytes
options.explanation: An empirical risk of < 2% occurs when the FATHER is the balanced der(14;21) carrier due to impaired motility and selection against unbalanced sperm, not when the mother is the carrier.

options.text: Essentially 100%; maternal balanced 14;21 translocations inevitably produce unbalanced gametes due to univalent arrest
options.explanation: Balanced carriers produce normal and balanced gametes in addition to unbalanced gametes; recurrence is far below 100%.

explanation: The mother is a balanced carrier of a Robertsonian der(14;21) translocation. During meiosis I, the translocated chromosome pairs with chromosomes 14 and 21 to form a trivalent structure. Theoretical segregation yields 6 possible gametic types: normal (14, 21), balanced translocation der(14;21), translocated trisomy 21 (der[14;21], 21), monosomy 21 (14), trisomy 14 (der[14;21], 14), and monosomy 14 (21). Monosomies 14 and 21 and trisomy 14 are non-viable, leaving 3 viable theoretical gametic outcomes: normal, balanced carrier, and Down syndrome (theoretical risk 1 in 3, or 33%). However, the EMPIRICAL recurrence risk in liveborn offspring of female balanced der(14;21) carriers is approximately 10% to 15% (and < 2% if the father is the carrier). This marked discrepancy between theoretical (33%) and empirical (10-15%) risk arises because unbalanced trisomy 21 embryos frequently undergo spontaneous first-trimester embryonic resorption and miscarriage. subject: Biochemistry
topic: G-Protein Coupled Receptor ADP-Ribosylation Mechanics
stem: An experimental microbiologist investigates the intracellular signaling cascades targeted by bacterial exotoxins in intestinal epithelial cells. In an in vitro assay, enterocytes are exposed to an exotoxin that catalyzes the transfer of an ADP-ribose moiety from NAD+ to a specific alpha subunit of a heterotrimeric G-protein. This modification permanently inactivates the intrinsic GTPase activity of the alpha subunit, freezing it in an active, GTP-bound conformation. Intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels increase more than 50-fold, triggering protein kinase A (PKA) phosphorylation of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) channel. Which of the following specific G-protein alpha subunits and targeting exotoxins is described in this experiment?

options.text: G-alpha-i subunit targeted by Bordetella pertussis toxin
options.explanation: Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates G-alpha-i (locking it in an inactive GDP-bound state), which prevents it from inhibiting adenylyl cyclase; however, the mechanism described (locking an active subunit via intrinsic GTPase ablation) is specific to G-alpha-s by cholera toxin.

options.text: G-alpha-s subunit targeted by Vibrio cholerae enterotoxin (choleragen)
options.explanation: Correct. Cholera toxin (produced by Vibrio cholerae) is an A-B toxin that ADP-ribosylates the G-alpha-s subunit of heterotrimeric G-proteins. This covalent modification blocks the intrinsic GTPase activity of G-alpha-s, preventing the hydrolysis of GTP to GDP. Consequently, G-alpha-s remains constitutively active, driving persistent adenylyl cyclase activation, massive intracellular cAMP elevation, PKA-mediated CFTR channel opening, and voluminous secretory diarrhea. In contrast, pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates and INHIBITS G-alpha-i, disabling the 'inhibitory' brake.

options.text: G-alpha-q subunit targeted by Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin
options.explanation: Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin is a phospholipase C (lecithinase) enzyme that hydrolyzes membrane sphingomyelin and phosphatidylcholine, not an ADP-ribosylating toxin of G-alpha-q.

options.text: G-alpha-t (transducin) subunit targeted by Bacillus anthracis lethal factor
options.explanation: Anthrax lethal factor is a zinc metalloproteinase that cleaves MAP kinase kinase (MAPKK/MEK), while anthrax edema factor is an adenylyl cyclase itself; neither targets transducin.

options.text: G-alpha-12/13 subunit targeted by Pseudomonas aeruginosa exotoxin A
options.explanation: Pseudomonas exotoxin A ADP-ribosylates eukaryotic elongation factor-2 (eEF-2) to arrest host ribosome protein synthesis; it does not target heterotrimeric G-protein subunits.

explanation: Correct. Cholera toxin (produced by Vibrio cholerae) is an A-B toxin that ADP-ribosylates the G-alpha-s subunit of heterotrimeric G-proteins. This covalent modification blocks the intrinsic GTPase activity of G-alpha-s, preventing the hydrolysis of GTP to GDP. Consequently, G-alpha-s remains constitutively active, driving persistent adenylyl cyclase activation, massive intracellular cAMP elevation, PKA-mediated CFTR channel opening, and voluminous secretory diarrhea. In contrast, pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates and INHIBITS G-alpha-i, disabling the 'inhibitory' brake. Inhibition of intrinsic GTPase locks G-alpha-s in active state -> Vibrio cholerae cholera toxin.

Inhibition of intrinsic GTPase locks G-alpha-s in active state -> Vibrio cholerae cholera toxin.

subject: Genetics
topic: Hereditary Hemochromatosis HFE Mutation and Hepcidin Regulation
stem: A 48-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, generalized joint pain predominantly in the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints, and erectile dysfunction. Physical examination reveals mild hepatomegaly and slate-gray hyperpigmentation over the sun-exposed areas of his neck and arms. Fasting laboratory evaluation demonstrates serum ferritin 1,850 ng/mL (normal: 20-250 ng/mL) and transferrin saturation 78% (normal: 20-50%). Genetic testing confirms homozygous C282Y missense mutations in the HFE gene on chromosome 6. In this patient, the mutant HFE protein fails to interact normally with transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) on hepatocytes. Which of the following molecular downstream consequences directly mediates the excessive systemic iron accumulation in this condition?

options.text: Hypersecretion of hepcidin by Kupffer cells causing widespread lysosomal ferroportin internalization and degradation
options.explanation: High hepcidin degrades ferroportin and traps iron inside enterocytes and macrophages, which is the hallmark of anemia of chronic disease, the exact opposite of hemochromatosis.

options.text: Constitutive transcriptional upregulation of luminal divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) independently of iron regulatory proteins
options.explanation: DMT1 is regulated by iron response elements (IRE/IRP) and mediates apical enterocyte Fe2+ uptake, but the primary genetic pathophysiology of HFE hemochromatosis operates via hepatic hepcidin suppression.

options.text: Inappropriately suppressed hepatic hepcidin synthesis leading to unrestrained basolateral enterocyte ferroportin export
options.explanation: Correct. In normal physiology, the HFE protein forms a regulatory complex with transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) and transferrin receptor 2 (TfR2) on the hepatocyte surface. When iron-loaded transferrin binds, HFE dissociates and stimulates the BMP-SMAD signaling cascade to synthesize HEPCIDIN. In hereditary hemochromatosis (homozygous C282Y mutation), the defective HFE protein cannot complex with TfR, falsely sensing systemic iron deficiency. Consequently, hepatocytes produce inappropriately LOW levels of hepcidin despite massive total body iron overload. Low hepcidin allows FERROPORTIN on basolateral duodenal enterocytes and reticuloendothelial macrophages to remain open, driving uninhibited systemic iron absorption and release.

options.text: Defective ceruloplasmin ferroxidase activity preventing oxidation of ferrous iron into transferrin-bound ferric iron
options.explanation: Ceruloplasmin deficiency causes aceruloplasminemia (a rare copper/iron disorder with neurologic degeneration), not classic HFE-associated hereditary hemochromatosis.

options.text: Impaired transferrin endocytosis in bone marrow erythroblasts causing secondary parenchymal iron deposition
options.explanation: Bone marrow transferrin uptake is intact in hemochromatosis; the defect is excessive intestinal absorption driven by low circulating hepcidin.

explanation: Correct. In normal physiology, the HFE protein forms a regulatory complex with transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) and transferrin receptor 2 (TfR2) on the hepatocyte surface. subject: Genetics
topic: Mitochondrial Heteroplasmy and MELAS Phenotypic Variability
stem: A 16-year-old girl is admitted to the neurology service with acute right-sided hemiparesis, expressive aphasia, and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Brain MRI reveals cortical and subcortical hyperintensities in the left temporal and parietal lobes that cross classic arterial vascular distributions. Serum lactate is markedly elevated at 5.2 mmol/L (normal: 0.5-2.0 mmol/L). Muscle biopsy demonstrates ragged-red fibers on Gomori trichrome stain. Genetic analysis reveals an m.3243A>G point mutation in the MT-TL1 gene encoding mitochondrial tRNALeu. Family history reveals that the patient's mother suffers only from mild bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, her maternal grandmother died in her 70s with adult-onset type 2 diabetes mellitus, and her younger brother has severe intractable infantile epilepsy. Which of the following genetic concepts best accounts for the marked differences in clinical severity observed among family members harboring this mutation?

options.text: Uniparental disomy of maternal chromosome 15 resulting in genomic imprinting defects
options.explanation: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 causes Angelman syndrome, an autosomal imprinting disorder unrelated to mitochondrial DNA mutations or ragged-red fibers.

options.text: Variable expressivity driven strictly by dynamic trinucleotide repeat expansion during maternal oogenesis
options.explanation: Trinucleotide repeat anticipation occurs in nuclear genes (e.g., Huntington disease, Fragile X), not in circular mitochondrial DNA.

options.text: Skewed X-chromosome inactivation (lyonization) favoring expression of the mutant allele in high-energy tissues
options.explanation: Mitochondrial DNA is maternally inherited through oocyte cytoplasm and is completely independent of nuclear X-chromosome inactivation.

options.text: Variable heteroplasmy across cellular mitochondrial genomes reaching critical tissue-specific metabolic thresholds
options.explanation: Correct. MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes) is a maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), most commonly m.3243A>G in MT-TL1. Mitochondria replicate independently and are distributed randomly during cell division (replicative segregation). A single cell can contain a mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA molecules, a state termed HETEROPLASMY. Clinical manifestations develop only when the proportion of mutant mtDNA exceeds a critical tissue threshold (threshold effect). Tissues with high oxidative metabolic demand (brain, skeletal muscle, cochlea, pancreatic beta-cells) are most vulnerable, explaining why family members with different mutant proportions exhibit vastly different phenotypic severities.

options.text: Locus heterogeneity where mutations in distinct unlinked nuclear genes produce overlapping encephalopathic phenotypes
options.explanation: Locus heterogeneity refers to mutations at different genetic loci causing the same disorder, whereas this family shares the identical m.3243A>G mtDNA mutation displaying variable severity due to heteroplasmy.

explanation: Correct. MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes) is a maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), most commonly m.3243A>G in MT-TL1. Mitochondria replicate independently and are distributed randomly during cell division (replicative segregation). A single cell can contain a mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA molecules, a state termed HETEROPLASMY. Clinical manifestations develop only when the proportion of mutant mtDNA exceeds a critical tissue threshold (threshold effect). Tissues with high oxidative metabolic demand (brain, skeletal muscle, cochlea, pancreatic beta-cells) are most vulnerable, explaining why family members with different mutant proportions exhibit vastly different phenotypic severities. Maternally inherited mtDNA mutation with ragged-red fibers + variable family severity -> Heteroplasmy threshold effect.

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Sphingolipidoses Differentiation Tay-Sachs vs Niemann-Pick
stem: A 7-month-old Ashkenazi Jewish boy is evaluated for progressive developmental regression. He previously rolled over and reached for toys, but over the past 2 months he has lost head control, ceased smiling, and demonstrates an exaggerated startle response to clapping and sudden noises (hyperacusis). Funduscopic examination reveals prominent bilateral cherry-red spots on the macula surrounded by pale retinal edema. Abdominal examination reveals a soft, non-tender abdomen with normal liver span and no palpable splenomegaly. Neurological examination reveals profound axial hypotonia and generalized motor weakness. Which of the following accumulated metabolic substrates and deficient enzymes is primarily responsible for this child's neurodegenerative condition?

options.text: Accumulation of sphingomyelin secondary to acid sphingomyelinase deficiency
options.explanation: Sphingomyelin accumulation (Niemann-Pick disease Type A) produces an identical cherry-red spot and developmental delay, but is definitively characterized by marked hepatosplenomegaly, which is completely absent here.

options.text: Accumulation of galactocerebroside secondary to galactocerebrosidase deficiency
options.explanation: Galactocerebrosidase deficiency causes Krabbe disease, characterized by peripheral neuropathy, extreme optic atrophy, globoid cells, and irritability, without cherry-red spots or hepatosplenomegaly.

options.text: Accumulation of glucocerebroside secondary to beta-glucocerebrosidase deficiency
options.explanation: Beta-glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease, which presents with hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and bone crises with 'wrinkled tissue paper' lipid-laden macrophages, without macular cherry-red spots.

options.text: Accumulation of ceramide trihexoside secondary to alpha-galactosidase A deficiency
options.explanation: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease, an X-linked disorder presenting with angiokeratomas, burning acroparesthesias, hypohidrosis, and renal/cardiovascular failure, not infantile neurodegeneration with cherry-red spots.

options.text: Accumulation of GM2 ganglioside secondary to beta-hexosaminidase A enzyme deficiency
options.explanation: Correct. Tay-Sachs disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage sphingolipidosis caused by deficiency of BETA-HEXOSAMINIDASE A, leading to pathological accumulation of GM2 GANGLIOSIDE within neuronal lysosomes. Clinical onset begins at 3 to 6 months with progressive motor loss, developmental regression, hyperacusis (acoustic startle), seizures, and macular cherry-red spots. Crucially, on USMLE Step 1, TAY-SACHS DISEASE HAS NO HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY. In contrast, Niemann-Pick disease (sphingomyelinase deficiency with sphingomyelin accumulation) features an identical macular cherry-red spot and neurodegeneration, but PROMINENT HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY.

explanation: Correct. Tay-Sachs disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage sphingolipidosis caused by deficiency of BETA-HEXOSAMINIDASE A, leading to pathological accumulation of GM2 GANGLIOSIDE within neuronal lysosomes. Clinical onset begins at 3 to 6 months with progressive motor loss, developmental regression, hyperacusis (acoustic startle), seizures, and macular cherry-red spots. In contrast, Niemann-Pick disease (sphingomyelinase deficiency with sphingomyelin accumulation) features an identical macular cherry-red spot and neurodegeneration, but PROMINENT HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY. Infant regression + hyperacusis + cherry-red spot + NO hepatosplenomegaly -> Tay-Sachs (beta-hexosaminidase A / GM2 ganglioside).

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Homocystinuria Cystathionine Beta-Synthase Deficiency vs Methionine Synthase
stem: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with acute right-sided hemiparesis and facial droop. Brain MRI confirms an acute ischemic stroke in the left middle cerebral artery distribution. He is tall and thin with long, slender fingers, pectus excavatum, and mild intellectual disability. Slit-lamp ophthalmological examination reveals inferomedial subluxation (downward dislocation) of both ocular lenses. Quantitative plasma amino acid chromatography reveals marked elevation of plasma total homocysteine (185 mcmol/L; normal < 15) and markedly elevated plasma methionine (240 mcmol/L; normal 15-40). Plasma methylmalonic acid concentration is normal. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies and required vitamin cofactors is the primary cause of this patient's condition?

options.text: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency requiring pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) cofactor supplementation
options.explanation: Correct. Classical homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism caused by deficiency of CYSTATHIONINE BETA-SYNTHASE (CBS), which normally condenses homocysteine and serine into cystathionine using PYRIDOXAL PHOSPHATE (VITAMIN B6) as an essential cofactor. When CBS is deficient, homocysteine accumulates and is trans-methylated back to methionine, leading to MARKEDLY ELEVATED PLASMA METHIONINE AND HOMOCYSTEINE. Clinical hallmark: marfanoid habitus, downward lens subluxation (ectopia lentis; contrast with Marfan upward dislocation), intellectual disability, and life-threatening premature thromboembolism (strokes, myocardial infarctions). In contrast, methionine synthase (MTR) deficiency causes homocystinuria with DECREASED methionine.

options.text: Methionine synthase deficiency requiring cobalamin (vitamin B12) cofactor supplementation
options.explanation: Methionine synthase converts homocysteine to methionine using vitamin B12; deficiency of this enzyme results in elevated homocysteine but LOW or low-normal plasma methionine, directly contradicting the marked hypermethioninemia observed in this patient.

options.text: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) deficiency requiring folate cofactor supplementation
options.explanation: MTHFR generates 5-methyl-THF required by methionine synthase; MTHFR deficiency causes hyperhomocysteinemia with LOW plasma methionine, unlike the high methionine seen here.

options.text: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency requiring adenosylcobalamin cofactor supplementation
options.explanation: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency causes methylmalonic acidemia with severe ketoacidosis, hyperammonemia, and high methylmalonic acid, which was explicitly normal in this patient.

options.text: Fibrillin-1 structural glycoprotein mutation altering transforming growth factor-beta regulation
options.explanation: Fibrillin-1 mutation causes Marfan syndrome (upward lens subluxation, normal intellect, normal amino acids, and aortic root dilation), not hyperhomocysteinemia, stroke, or downward lens dislocation.

explanation: Correct. Classical homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism caused by deficiency of CYSTATHIONINE BETA-SYNTHASE (CBS), which normally condenses homocysteine and serine into cystathionine using PYRIDOXAL PHOSPHATE (VITAMIN B6) as an essential cofactor. When CBS is deficient, homocysteine accumulates and is trans-methylated back to methionine, leading to MARKEDLY ELEVATED PLASMA METHIONINE AND HOMOCYSTEINE. Clinical hallmark: marfanoid habitus, downward lens subluxation (ectopia lentis; contrast with Marfan upward dislocation), intellectual disability, and life-threatening premature thromboembolism (strokes, myocardial infarctions). In contrast, methionine synthase (MTR) deficiency causes homocystinuria with DECREASED methionine. Marfanoid + stroke + downward lens ectopia + high homocysteine AND high methionine -> Cystathionine beta-synthase (vitamin B6).

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Xeroderma Pigmentosum Nucleotide Excision Repair Pyrimidine Dimers
stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the dermatology clinic by his parents because of severe, blistering sunburns that develop after even minimal sun exposure (less than 10 minutes outdoors). Physical examination reveals extensive solar lentigines (freckling), poikiloderma, cutaneous xerosis, and prominent telangiectasias over the face, neck, and forearms. Biopsy of a pigmented papule on his cheek reveals an invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Cultured skin fibroblasts are exposed to ultraviolet-C radiation in vitro. Analysis of cellular DNA demonstrates persistent cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and 6-4 photoproducts that fail to be excised. Which of the following specific DNA repair enzymes is primarily defective in this patient?

options.text: DNA mismatch repair endonuclease (MSH2/MLH1) that recognizes single-base replication mispairings
options.explanation: Mismatch repair (MMR) corrects replication proofreading errors (single-base mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops); defects cause Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer), not UV dimer repair failure.

options.text: UV-specific excinuclease (endonuclease) that cleaves phosphodiester bonds flanking the DNA lesion
options.explanation: Correct. Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective NUCLEOTIDE EXCISION REPAIR (NER). Ultraviolet (UV) radiation induces covalent cross-linking between adjacent pyrimidine bases (thymine-thymine or thymine-cytosine cyclobutane dimers), distorting the DNA double helix. NER operates via: (1) Recognition of helical distortion by XP proteins; (2) Cleavage of the damaged DNA strand at phosphodiester bonds on both the 5' and 3' sides of the lesion by a UV-SPECIFIC ENDONUCLEASE (excinuclease complex); (3) Excision of the ~24-32 nucleotide oligomer; and (4) Resynthesis by DNA polymerase and sealing by DNA ligase. Defective endonuclease activity leaves pyrimidine dimers unexcised, resulting in replication block, accumulation of mutations, and a >10,000-fold increased risk of non-melanoma skin cancer and melanoma before age 10.

options.text: DNA glycosylase that cleaves the N-glycosidic bond of oxidized or deaminated purines
options.explanation: DNA glycosylases initiate base excision repair (BER) by removing single chemically altered bases (e.g., uracil formed from cytosine deamination, or 8-oxoguanine), not bulky UV photoproducts.

options.text: Non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer and DNA-dependent protein kinase
options.explanation: NHEJ repairs double-strand DNA breaks induced by ionizing radiation (X-rays, gamma rays); defective NHEJ causes ataxia-telangiectasia and severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), not xeroderma pigmentosum.

options.text: Homologous recombination repair protein ATM/BRCA1 that pairs with sister chromatid templates
options.explanation: Homologous recombination repairs double-strand breaks during the S and G2 phases of the cell cycle; defects in BRCA1/2 increase breast and ovarian cancer, while ATM defects cause ataxia-telangiectasia.

explanation: Correct. Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective NUCLEOTIDE EXCISION REPAIR (NER). Ultraviolet (UV) radiation induces covalent cross-linking between adjacent pyrimidine bases (thymine-thymine or thymine-cytosine cyclobutane dimers), distorting the DNA double helix. NER operates via: (1) Recognition of helical distortion by XP proteins; (2) Cleavage of the damaged DNA strand at phosphodiester bonds on both the 5' and 3' sides of the lesion by a UV-SPECIFIC ENDONUCLEASE (excinuclease complex); (3) Excision of the ~24-32 nucleotide oligomer; and (4) Resynthesis by DNA polymerase and sealing by DNA ligase. subject: Biochemistry
topic: Alkaptonuria Homogentisate 1,2-Dioxygenase Deficiency and Ochronosis
stem: A 52-year-old man presents with chronic, debilitating pain and stiffness in his lower back, hips, and knees. He reports that his urine has always turned dark black when left standing in the toilet bowl for several hours. Physical examination reveals dark blue-black pigmentation over the sclerae of both eyes and the cartilaginous pinnae of his ears. Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine demonstrate severe narrowing of the intervertebral disc spaces with dense calcification of the intervertebral discs throughout the entire lumbar spine. A fresh urine sample is initially normal amber in color, but upon alkalinization and prolonged air exposure, it oxidizes to a dense black color. Which of the following enzymes in the amino acid catabolic pathway is deficient in this patient?

options.text: Phenylalanine hydroxylase in the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine

topic: Maple Syrup Urine Disease Branched-Chain Alpha-Ketoacid Dehydrogenase
stem: A 5-day-old female infant is brought to the emergency department because of poor feeding, progressive lethargy, and episodic hypertonicity with bicycling movements of her lower extremities. The infant was born full-term following an uneventful pregnancy and was healthy for the first 48 hours of life after initiating breastfeeding. On physical examination, she is stuporous and alternating between muscular hypotonia and hypertonicity. Her diapers have a distinctive sweet, burnt-sugar odor. Laboratory evaluation reveals marked metabolic acidosis with an elevated anion gap, severe ketosis, and a plasma ammonia concentration of 110 mcmol/L (mild elevation). Plasma amino acid analysis reveals markedly elevated concentrations of leucine, isoleucine, and valine, with detection of alloisoleucine. Which of the following cofactors is an essential catalytic component of the deficient multienzyme complex in this infant?

options.text: Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6)
options.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate is required for transamination reactions (aminotransferases) and cystathionine beta-synthase, but not for oxidative decarboxylation by BCKDH.

options.text: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)
options.explanation: Tetrahydrobiopterin is the cofactor for phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan hydroxylases, as well as nitric oxide synthase, not branched-chain ketoacid decarboxylation.

options.text: Biotin (vitamin B7)
options.explanation: Biotin serves as the cofactor for carboxylase enzymes (pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase), not the BCKDH oxidative decarboxylase complex.

The sweet burnt-sugar odor is due to isoleucine derivatives (alloisoleucine is pathognomonic). options.explanation: Adenosylcobalamin is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; it is not utilized in the BCKDH reaction.

topic: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase Deficiency and Splenic Degmacytes
stem: A 24-year-old African American man presents to the urgent care clinic with fatigue, scleral icterus, and dark mahogany-colored urine 3 days after completing a course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a skin abscess. Supravital staining with crystal violet demonstrates dark, round intracellular inclusions adherent to red blood cell membranes (Heinz bodies). options.text: Conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate by pyruvate kinase in glycolysis
options.explanation: Pyruvate kinase deficiency impairs ATP generation in glycolysis, causing chronic non-spherocytic extravascular hemolytic anemia with echinocytes (burr cells), without Heinz bodies or bite cells.

options.text: Oxidation of glucose to sorbitol by aldose reductase in the polyol pathway
options.explanation: Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol; its hyperactivation in hyperglycemia causes osmotic damage in diabetic cataracts and neuropathy, not hemolytic bite cells.

options.explanation: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) deficiency causes Tarui disease (glycogen storage disease Type VII), presenting with exercise-induced muscle cramps and exertional hemolysis, not oxidant-induced Heinz body bite cells.

options.text: Dephosphorylation of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate by bisphosphoglycerate phosphatase in the Luebering-Rapoport shunt
options.explanation: The Luebering-Rapoport glycolytic shunt regulates 2,3-BPG concentration and oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve affinity; it does not protect against oxidant stress or generate bite cells.

options.text: Reduction of NADP+ to NADPH by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in the hexose monophosphate shunt
options.explanation: Correct. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) catalyzes the rate-limiting first step of the pentose phosphate (hexose monophosphate) shunt: the oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphoglucono-delta-lactone, with the simultaneous REDUCTION OF NADP+ TO NADPH. Because mature erythrocytes lack nuclei and mitochondria, the HMP shunt is their SOLE SOURCE OF NADPH. NADPH is essential to regenerate reduced glutathione (GSH) from oxidized glutathione (GSSG) via glutathione reductase. When exposed to oxidant stress (sulfonamides, fava beans, dapsone, primaquine, infections), GSH is depleted, allowing reactive oxygen species to cross-link sulfhydryl groups on hemoglobin chains. Denatured hemoglobin precipitates into insoluble clumps termed HEINZ BODIES. As erythrocytes transit the splenic cords, splenic red pulp macrophages phagocytose these rigid inclusions, leaving behind characteristic 'BITE CELLS' (degmacytes).

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Acute Intermittent Porphyria Porphobilinogen Deaminase Deficiency
stem: A 28-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital with severe, colicky abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting that began 2 days after starting a low-carbohydrate fasting diet and taking oral rifampin for latent tuberculosis. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender to deep palpation, without rebound or guarding. Neurological examination reveals mild proximal upper extremity motor weakness, anxiety, and auditory hallucinations. A fresh urine specimen collected in a clear container appears normal light yellow, but turns deep reddish-purple (port-wine color) after 2 hours of exposure to ambient sunlight. Quantitative urinalysis demonstrates markedly elevated concentrations of delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG). options.text: Porphobilinogen deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase)
options.explanation: Correct. Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is an autosomal dominant disorder of heme biosynthesis caused by deficiency of PORPHOBILINOGEN DEAMINASE (PBGD; also known as hydroxymethylbilane synthase). Clinical attacks are characterized by the classic 5 Ps: Painful abdomen (severe neurovisceral pain disproportionate to exam), Port-wine colored urine, Polyneuropathy (predominantly proximal motor weakness), Psychological disturbances (delirium, hallucinations, anxiety), and Precipitated by drugs (CYP450 inducers like rifampin, barbiturates, antiepileptics), fasting, or alcohol. These triggers induce hepatic ALA SYNTHASE-1, driving accumulation of neurotoxic intermediates: delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG). CRUCIALLY, BECAUSE THE ENZYMATIC BLOCK OCCURS PRIOR TO THE FORMATION OF CYCLIC PORPHYRINOGENS, AIP HAS ABSOLUTELY NO CUTANEOUS PHOTOSENSITIVITY OR BLISTERING. In contrast, porphyria cutanea tarda (uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency) occurs AFTER porphyrin ring closure and presents with prominent cutaneous blistering and hypertrichosis.

options.text: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase in the conversion of uroporphyrinogen III to coproporphyrinogen III
options.explanation: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT), which is characterized by marked cutaneous photosensitivity, vesicles, bullae, and skin fragility on sun-exposed areas, without acute neurovisceral crises.

options.text: Ferrochelatase in the final insertion of ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX
options.explanation: Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria, characterized by painful, non-blistering burning photosensitivity in early childhood, not acute episodic neurovisceral pain with proximal weakness.

options.text: ALA dehydratase (porphobilinogen synthase) in the condensation of two molecules of ALA
options.explanation: ALA dehydratase deficiency is an extremely rare recessive porphyria (or caused by lead toxicity); while it causes neurovisceral symptoms, lead inhibits both ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, elevating ALA without porphobilinogen.

options.text: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase in the cyclization of hydroxymethylbilane
options.explanation: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency causes congenital erythropoietic porphyria (Gunther disease), an infantile disorder with severe hemolytic anemia, extreme cutaneous mutilating photosensitivity, and red teeth (erythrodontia).

topic: Familial Hypercholesterolemia LDL Receptor Endocytosis Defect
stem: A 19-year-old college student presents with nodular, firm, painless swellings over both Achilles tendons and prominent yellowish papules along the extensor surfaces of his elbows. Slit-lamp examination demonstrates bilateral corneal arcus. His father died suddenly of an acute myocardial infarction at age 38, and his paternal grandfather had coronary bypass surgery at age 42. Fasting lipid panel reveals: Total Cholesterol 580 mg/dL, Triglycerides 140 mg/dL, HDL Cholesterol 46 mg/dL, and LDL Cholesterol 506 mg/dL. Genetic sequencing reveals an autosomal dominant mutation in the low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor gene that prevents the receptor from concentrating into clathrin-coated pits on the hepatocyte plasma membrane. Which of the following cell biological processes is primarily disrupted as a consequence of this mutation?

options.text: Hydrolysis of chylomicron core triglycerides by capillary endothelial lipoprotein lipase
options.explanation: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) or ApoC-II deficiency causes Type I familial chylomicronemia, presenting with eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis, acute pancreatitis, and massive hypertriglyceridemia, not pure hypercholesterolemia with tendon xanthomas.

options.text: Receptor-mediated endocytosis of apolipoprotein B-100-containing lipoprotein particles
options.explanation: Correct. Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH; Type IIa dyslipidemia) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused most commonly by mutations in the LDL RECEPTOR (LDLR) gene on chromosome 19. Normal cellular uptake of LDL involves: (1) Binding of apolipoprotein B-100 on the LDL particle surface to the extracellular domain of LDLR; (2) Lateral clustering of the ligand-receptor complexes into CLATHRIN-COATED PITS on the cell membrane; (3) Invagination and pinch-off via dynamin to form coated vesicles; (4) Endosomal acidification, prompting LDL release and receptor recycling. Mutations in the cytoplasmic tail of the LDL receptor (Class 4 LDLR mutations) prevent interaction with adaptor proteins (e.g., ARH/AP-2), preventing receptor concentration into clathrin-coated pits. As a result, RECEPTOR-MEDIATED ENDOCYTOSIS IS IMPAIRED, leading to profound accumulation of circulating atherogenic LDL, early coronary artery disease, tendon xanthomas, and corneal arcus.

options.text: Esterification of free cholesterol in high-density lipoproteins by lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase
options.explanation: Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) deficiency impairs HDL maturation and cholesterol reverse transport, leading to corneal opacities, target cells, hemolytic anemia, and renal failure, not isolated extreme LDL elevation.

options.text: Hepatic microsomal triglyceride transfer protein assembly of nascent very-low-density lipoproteins
options.explanation: Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) deficiency causes abetalipoproteinemia, characterized by absent apoB-48 and apoB-100, fat malabsorption, acanthocytosis, and undetectable serum cholesterol/LDL.

options.text: Apolipoprotein E-mediated hepatic clearance of remnant chylomicrons and intermediate-density lipoproteins
options.explanation: Defective ApoE (homozygous ApoE2) causes Type III dysbetalipoproteinemia (familial dysbetalipoproteinemia), presenting with elevated chylomicron/VLDL remnants, tuberoeruptive and palmar xanthomas, and both elevated cholesterol and triglycerides.

topic: Glycogen Storage Disease Type I von Gierke vs Type III Cori
stem: A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatric clinic because of generalized lethargy, tachypnea, and prominent abdominal distension. Physical examination reveals a rounded 'doll-like' facial appearance with fat cheeks, thin extremities, and massive hepatomegaly (liver edge palpable 6 cm below the right costal margin); the spleen is not palpable. Fasting laboratory evaluation demonstrates: - Blood Glucose: 34 mg/dL (severe hypoglycemia) - Blood Lactate: 6.8 mmol/L (normal: 0.5-2.0 mmol/L; marked lactic acidosis) - Serum Uric Acid: 10.4 mg/dL (normal: 2.0-5.5 mg/dL; marked hyperuricemia) - Serum Triglycerides: 540 mg/dL (marked hyperlipidemia) Intravenous administration of glucagon fails to increase blood glucose concentration, but causes a further surge in blood lactate levels. Liver biopsy demonstrates hepatocytes distended with structurally normal glycogen and marked steatosis. Which of the following enzymes is primarily deficient in this infant?

options.text: Debranching enzyme (alpha-1,6-glucosidase) in the breakdown of glycogen branch points
options.explanation: Debranching enzyme deficiency (Type III Cori disease) presents with hepatomegaly and hypoglycemia, but has NORMAL blood lactate and intact gluconeogenesis, whereas this infant has profound lactic acidosis and hyperuricemia.

options.text: Branching enzyme (amylo-1,4 to 1,6-transglucosidase) in the synthesis of glycogen branches
options.explanation: Branching enzyme deficiency (Type IV Andersen disease) leads to abnormal glycogen with few branch points (polyglucosan bodies), causing infantile cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and death before age 2, without severe hypoglycemia.

options.text: Glucose-6-phosphatase in the terminal step of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis
options.explanation: Correct. Glycogen storage disease Type I (von Gierke disease) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of GLUCOSE-6-PHOSPHATASE (Type Ia) or the glucose-6-phosphate translocase (Type Ib). Glucose-6-phosphatase catalyzes the final, shared step of BOTH glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis: hydrolyzing glucose-6-phosphate into free glucose and inorganic phosphate in the endoplasmic reticulum of liver and kidney cells. When deficient, free glucose cannot be released into the blood, causing SEVERE FASTING HYPOGLYCEMIA. Accumulated G6P is shunted into alternate pathways: (1) Glycolysis -> excessive pyruvate and LACTIC ACIDOSIS (lactate competes with urate at renal OAT1 transporters -> HYPERURICEMIA and gout); (2) HMP shunt -> excessive ribose-5-phosphate, driving de novo purine synthesis and hyperuricemia; (3) Lipogenesis -> marked HYPERTRIGLYCERIDEMIA and hepatic steatosis ('doll-like' facies, massive hepatomegaly). CRUCIAL STEP 1 DISTINCTION: In von Gierke disease, GLUCAGON FAILS TO INCREASE GLUCOSE, BUT INCREASES LACTATE. In contrast, Type III (Cori disease; debranching enzyme deficiency) has NORMAL BLOOD LACTATE, intact gluconeogenesis, and abnormal limit dextrin-like glycogen.

options.text: Lysosomal alpha-1,4-glucosidase (acid maltase) in the vacuolar degradation of glycogen
options.explanation: Acid maltase deficiency (Type II Pompe disease) causes lysosomal glycogen accumulation resulting in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, profound hypotonia, and early cardiorespiratory failure, without hypoglycemia or lactic acidosis.

options.text: Liver glycogen phosphorylase in the phosphorolytic cleavage of alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds
options.explanation: Liver glycogen phosphorylase deficiency (Type VI Hers disease) presents with benign mild fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly, but without the severe metabolic derangements (lactic acidosis, marked hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia) seen in von Gierke disease.

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Lesch-Nyhan Syndrome HGPRT Deficiency and Purine Salvage Failure
stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric genetics clinic because of involuntary muscle twisting, developmental regression, and aggressive behavioral abnormalities. His mother notes that over the past 3 months, he has repeatedly bitten his own lips, tongue, and fingertips, requiring arm splints and dental extraction to prevent severe tissue loss. Examination reveals dystonia, choreoathetosis, hyperreflexia with bilateral ankle clonus, and severe self-mutilation injuries to the lower lip and digits. His diapers frequently contain an orange sand-like substance. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates serum uric acid 12.8 mg/dL (normal: 2.0-5.5 mg/dL). Enzyme assay of cultured skin fibroblasts confirms complete absence of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) activity. Which of the following regulatory enzymes in purine metabolism exhibits a marked compensatory increase in activity as a direct consequence of this salvage pathway defect?

options.text: Xanthine oxidase in the oxidation of hypoxanthine to xanthine and uric acid
options.explanation: Xanthine oxidase catalyzes uric acid production and is inhibited by allopurinol/febuxostat, but the primary regulatory enzyme that undergoes massive compensatory allosteric upregulation is PRPP amidotransferase.

options.text: Adenosine deaminase in the irreversible deamination of adenosine to inosine
options.explanation: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) due to toxic dATP accumulation in lymphocytes; ADA activity is not the driver of Lesch-Nyhan purine overproduction.

options.text: Ribonucleotide reductase in the reduction of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Ornithine Transcarbamylase Deficiency vs UMP Synthase Deficiency
stem: A 3-day-old male newborn develops progressive somnolence, vomiting, and tachypnea. Arterial blood gas demonstrates respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.54, pCO2 24 mm Hg, HCO3- 20 mEq/L). Laboratory evaluation reveals a critical plasma ammonia concentration of 680 mcmol/L (normal: < 50 mcmol/L) and blood urea nitrogen of 2 mg/dL. Complete blood count demonstrates hemoglobin 16.2 g/dL and MCV 98 fL (normal for age, no megaloblastic changes). Quantitative urinary organic acid analysis reveals markedly elevated urinary orotic acid excretion (1,250 mcmol/mmol creatinine; normal < 5). Plasma amino acid chromatography demonstrates undetectable citrulline and elevated glutamine. Which of the following is the mode of inheritance and primary deficient enzyme in this infant?

options.text: Autosomal recessive inheritance of uridine monophosphate (UMP) synthase deficiency
options.explanation: UMP synthase deficiency (hereditary orotic aciduria) causes high urinary orotic acid, but ammonia levels are completely NORMAL, and infants present with profound megaloblastic anemia and failure to thrive, not neonatal hyperammonemic coma.

options.text: Autosomal recessive inheritance of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency
options.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I) deficiency causes severe neonatal hyperammonemia, but because carbamoyl phosphate cannot be formed, orotic acid levels are completely normal or low.

options.text: Autosomal recessive inheritance of argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency
options.explanation: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (citrullinemia Type I) causes hyperammonemia, but is characterized by MASSIVELY ELEVATED plasma citrulline, whereas citrulline is undetectable in OTC deficiency.

options.text: X-linked dominant inheritance of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency
options.explanation: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency impairs pyrimidine catabolism, causing severe toxic accumulation of 5-fluorouracil during chemotherapy; it does not cause neonatal hyperammonemia or orotic aciduria.

options.text: X-linked recessive inheritance of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency
options.explanation: Correct. Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is the most common inborn error of the urea cycle and the ONLY UREA CYCLE DEFECT WITH X-LINKED RECESSIVE INHERITANCE (all other urea cycle enzyme deficiencies are autosomal recessive). In the mitochondria, OTC normally condenses carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to produce citrulline. When OTC is deficient, carbamoyl phosphate accumulates in the mitochondria and overflows into the cytoplasm, where it enters the pyrimidine synthesis pathway, driving massive production and excretion of OROTIC ACID (orotic aciduria). The failure of the urea cycle causes severe, life-threatening HYPERAMMONEMIA with low/absent citrulline and low BUN. CRUCIAL STEP 1 DIFFERENTIATING CONCEPT: Orotic aciduria is also seen in hereditary orotic aciduria (UMP SYNTHASE DEFICIENCY). However, UMP synthase deficiency is autosomal recessive, has NORMAL AMMONIA, and features SEVERE MEGALOBLASTIC ANEMIA refractory to B12/folate. In contrast, OTC deficiency features SEVERE HYPERAMMONEMIA, normal blood counts, and X-linked inheritance.

topic: Sickle Cell Hemoglobin Molecular Polymerization Kinetics
stem: A 22-year-old African American man presents to the emergency department with severe, unremitting bone pain in his lower back, bilaterally in his femurs, and throughout his chest following a high-altitude hike in the Rocky Mountains. Physical examination demonstrates pale conjunctivae, mild scleral icterus, and extreme tenderness over the mid-shafts of both femurs. Laboratory evaluation reveals hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, reticulocyte count 11.2%, and indirect bilirubin 3.6 mg/dL. Peripheral blood smear demonstrates sickle-shaped erythrocytes, target cells, and Howell-Jolly bodies. Hemoglobin electrophoresis demonstrates 88% HbS, 10% HbF, and 2% HbA2 (homozygous HbSS). At the molecular structural level, the pathological sickling of deoxygenated HbS molecules is driven by which of the following biophysical interactions?

options.text: Formation of a hydrophobic protrusion by valine at position 6 that fits into a complementary hydrophobic pocket on an adjacent beta-globin chain
options.explanation: Correct. Sickle cell anemia (HbS) is caused by a single-base missense mutation (GAG to GTG in codon 6 of the beta-globin gene on chromosome 11), substituting non-polar, hydrophobic VALINE for negatively charged, hydrophilic GLUTAMATE on the outer surface of the beta-globin chain. In the oxygenated state (R-state), the hydrophobic valine residue remains exposed but innocuous. However, upon deoxygenation (T-state; triggered by hypoxia, acidosis, dehydration, high altitude), a conformational change unmasks a complementary hydrophobic receptor pocket (composed of phenylalanine 85 and leucine 88) on the beta chain of an adjacent deoxyhemoglobin tetramer. The mutant valine inserts into this hydrophobic pocket, driving non-covalent aggregation into rigid, insoluble crystalline polymers of 14-strand helical filaments. These polymers distort the erythrocyte into a rigid, fragile crescent (sickle cell), causing microvascular vaso-occlusion and extravascular/intravascular hemolysis.

options.text: Creation of an aberrant covalent disulfide bond between mutated cysteine residues on adjacent alpha- and beta-globin subunits
options.explanation: The HbS mutation involves valine, not cysteine; polymerization is mediated entirely by non-covalent hydrophobic interactions, not covalent disulfide cross-linking.

options.text: Disruption of the proximal histidine coordination bond with the heme iron atom causing constitutive methemoglobin formation
options.explanation: Mutation of the proximal (HisF8) or distal (HisE7) histidine residues causes Hemoglobin M disease (congenital methemoglobinemia), not sickle cell polymerization.

options.text: Electrostatic repulsion between positively charged lysine residues on neighboring beta-globin dimers
options.explanation: Substitution of glutamate with positively charged lysine at position 6 produces Hemoglobin C (HbC), which forms hexagonal intracellular crystals without forming sickle polymers or sickled erythrocytes.

options.text: Impaired allosteric binding of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate locking hemoglobin in a high-affinity relaxed quaternary conformation
options.explanation: HbS polymerization occurs exclusively in the low-affinity deoxygenated T-state; locking hemoglobin in the relaxed R-state (e.g., via fetal hemoglobin HbF or voxelotor) inhibits sickling.

topic: Osteogenesis Imperfecta Type I Collagen Glycine Substitution
stem: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric orthopedic clinic after sustaining a spiral fracture of her right tibia after slipping on carpet. Her medical history is remarkable for four prior low-impact fractures of long bones and a clavicle fracture during infancy. Physical examination demonstrates mild short stature, generalized joint hypermobility, and prominent blue sclerae in both eyes. Dental examination reveals small, misshapen, translucent, brownish-blue teeth that are prone to rapid wear (dentinogenesis imperfecta). Audiological testing demonstrates mild bilateral conductive hearing loss. Genetic testing confirms an autosomal dominant missense mutation in the COL1A1 gene encoding the pro-alpha-1 chain of Type I collagen. The substitution of which of the following amino acids by a bulkier residue is the primary molecular cause of defective collagen triple helix formation in this patient?

options.text: Proline, because its rigid pyrrolidine ring is required to form interchain covalent desmosine cross-links
options.explanation: Desmosine cross-links are unique to elastin, formed from lysine residues by lysyl oxidase, not proline in collagen.

options.text: Glycine, because its minimal hydrogen side chain is uniquely required for steric packing within the interior of the collagen triple helix
options.explanation: Correct. Type I collagen is the primary structural protein of bone, dentin, sclerae, tendons, and skin. It is synthesized as a triple helix composed of two pro-alpha-1 chains and one pro-alpha-2 chain. The primary amino acid sequence consists of an invariant repeating triplet motif: (Gly-X-Y)n, where X is frequently proline (which induces helical kinking) and Y is frequently hydroxyproline or hydroxylysine (which forms stabilizing interchain hydrogen bonds). GLYCINE IS THE SMALLEST AMINO ACID, possessing only a single hydrogen atom as its side chain. Because the core of the triple helix is extremely tight and crowded, ONLY GLYCINE CAN FIT INTO THE RESTRICTED INTERIOR AXIS. In osteogenesis imperfecta (OI Type I/II/III/IV), point mutations that replace glycine with bulkier or charged amino acids (e.g., alanine, aspartate, arginine) cause steric clash, preventing normal triple helix folding and assembly (dominant negative effect) or reducing collagen synthesis.

options.text: Lysine, because its epsilon-amino group is required for extracellular copper-dependent lysyl hydroxylase cleavage
options.explanation: Lysyl oxidase (not hydroxylase) requires copper, and lysyl hydroxylase operates intracellularly on lysine residues; however, the invariant core residue required for triple-helix packing is glycine.

options.text: Tryptophan, because its aromatic indole ring mediates hydrophobic base-stacking between neighboring tropocollagen fibrils
options.explanation: Type I collagen completely lacks tryptophan residues in its core triple-helical domain; the structural integrity relies on glycine.

options.text: Cysteine, because its sulfhydryl groups form essential intrachain disulfide bridges along the entire helical rod
options.explanation: Disulfide bridges are formed exclusively within the C-terminal propeptide extension to initiate triple-helix alignment, and are removed extracellularly; they do not run along the triple helix.

subject: Genetics
topic: Marfan Syndrome Fibrillin-1 Mutation and Excessive TGF-Beta Signaling
stem: A 17-year-old high school basketball player undergoes a pre-participation sports physical examination. He is 6 feet 6 inches (198 cm) tall, with an arm span of 206 cm (arm span-to-height ratio > 1.05) and long, slender arachnodactylic digits. He has a positive Steinberg thumb sign and a positive Walker-Murdoch wrist sign, along with moderate pectus excavatum. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy reveals bilateral superior and temporal (upward) dislocation of the crystalline lenses (ectopia lentis). Transthoracic echocardiography reveals marked dilatation of the aortic root (sinus of Valsalva diameter 46 mm) with mild aortic regurgitation. Genetic sequencing identifies a heterozygous mutation in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15 encoding fibrillin-1. In addition to structural microfibril scaffolding deficiency, which of the following aberrant cellular signaling mechanisms directly drives the aortic elastolysis and connective tissue pathology in this syndrome?

options.text: Constitutive autophosphorylation of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2) driving hypervascularization
options.explanation: VEGFR2 mediates angiogenesis in tumors and vascular malformations; it is not the pathogenic signaling axis dysregulated by fibrillin-1 mutations in Marfan syndrome.

options.text: Impaired lysyl oxidase cross-linking of collagen fibers secondary to copper transport defects in the trans-Golgi network
options.explanation: Impaired lysyl oxidase cross-linking due to copper transport deficiency causes Menkes disease (ATP7A mutation), characterized by kinky hair, hypotonia, and aneurysms, not classical Marfan syndrome.

options.text: Excessive activation of transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) signaling due to failure of extracellular matrix sequestration
options.explanation: Correct. Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by heterozygous mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes FIBRILLIN-1. Fibrillin-1 is a large glycoprotein that polymerizes to form extracellular microfibrils, which serve as the scaffolding for tropoelastin deposition in elastic tissues (aorta, periosteum, zonular fibers of the lens). Beyond its structural role, normal fibrillin-1 binds and sequesters the large latent TRANSFORMING GROWTH FACTOR-BETA (TGF-beta) complex in the extracellular matrix. Defective or deficient fibrillin-1 fails to sequester latent TGF-beta, resulting in UNRESTRAINED, EXCESSIVE BIOACTIVE TGF-BETA SIGNALING. Excessive TGF-beta stimulates vascular smooth muscle apoptosis, metalloproteinase (MMP) secretion, and progressive degradation of elastic lamellae (cystic medial necrosis) in the aortic root, driving aortic aneurysms and dissections.

options.text: Defective cleavage of procollagen amino- and carboxy-terminal propeptides in the extracellular space
options.explanation: Defective procollagen peptidase cleavage prevents mature collagen fibril assembly, which causes Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (arthrochalasia type), not Marfan syndrome.

options.text: Constitutive activation of fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) inhibiting chondrocyte proliferation
options.explanation: Activating FGFR3 mutations cause achondroplasia, the most common form of dwarfism, featuring rhizomelic limb shortening, not tall stature and aortic aneurysms.

subject: Genetics
topic: McCune-Albright Syndrome Postzygotic Somatic GNAS Mutation
stem: An 8-year-old girl is evaluated for precocious puberty and recurrent skeletal fractures. Over the past 6 months, her mother noted breast bud development, pubic hair, and two episodes of vaginal bleeding. Physical examination reveals a large, unilateral, irregularly bordered brown macule with jagged edges ('coast of Maine' border) spanning across her left flank and buttock, stopping abruptly at the midline. Skeletal survey reveals multiple radiolucent, ground-glass expansile bone lesions with cortical thinning (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia) involving the left femur and pelvis. Serum estradiol and free thyroxine levels are elevated with suppressed LH, FSH, and TSH. Genetic analysis of affected bone tissue reveals a postzygotic activating somatic missense mutation in the GNAS gene encoding the Gs alpha subunit. Which of the following genetic concepts explains why this mutation is survivable in this patient but would cause fatal embryonic lethality if present as a constitutional germline mutation?

options.text: Genomic imprinting with selective maternal allele inactivation in developing neural crest cells
options.explanation: Genomic imprinting involves parent-of-origin dependent methylation (e.g., Prader-Willi/Angelman), which does not account for the survival of McCune-Albright syndrome mutations.

options.text: Mitochondrial heteroplasmy with tissue-specific threshold variability across organ systems
options.explanation: McCune-Albright is caused by a nuclear chromosomal gene mutation (GNAS on chromosome 20), not mitochondrial circular DNA.

options.text: Anticipation driven by trinucleotide repeat expansion in maternal gametogenesis
options.explanation: Trinucleotide expansions (e.g., Huntington, Fragile X) cause dynamic anticipation, not mosaic survivability of lethal G-protein activating mutations.

options.text: Somatic mosaicism arising early in embryonic postzygotic development
options.explanation: Correct. McCune-Albright syndrome is a rare genetic disorder characterized by the classic clinical triad of: (1) Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (ground-glass bone lesions, pathological fractures); (2) Unilateral cafe-au-lait macules with jagged, irregular borders ('coast of Maine') that respect the midline; and (3) Autonomous endocrine hyperfunction (precocious puberty, thyrotoxicosis, Cushing syndrome, gigantism). The underlying etiology is an activating gain-of-function mutation in the GNAS gene, which encodes the G-alpha-s subunit of heterotrimeric G-proteins. This mutation abolishes intrinsic GTPase activity, leading to constitutive, ligand-independent adenylyl cyclase activation and continuous cAMP generation in target tissues. CRUCIAL GENETIC PRINCIPLE: If this mutation occurred in the germline (present in every cell of the conceptus), constitutive Gs signaling would cause fatal embryonic lethality. It is survivable ONLY BECAUSE IT ARISES AS A POSTZYGOTIC SOMATIC MUTATION, creating a MOSAIC distribution where only a fraction of tissues harbor the mutation while surrounding normal cells maintain viability.

options.text: Uniparental disomy of chromosome 20 leading to complete loss of heterozygosity
options.explanation: Uniparental disomy causes recessive disease unmasking or imprinting anomalies, not somatic activating gain-of-function mosaicism.

subject: Genetics
topic: Fragile X Syndrome FMR1 CGG Repeat Expansion Hypermethylation
stem: An 8-year-old boy is referred to a developmental pediatrician because of severe intellectual disability, speech delay, and repetitive hand-flapping behaviors. On physical examination, he avoids direct eye contact. He has a long, narrow face with a prominent forehead and jaw, large everted ears, high-arched palate, and marked hyperextensibility of his finger joints. Genital examination reveals bilateral macroorchidism (testicular volume > 25 mL; normal for age < 4 mL). Southern blot analysis reveals an unstable CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion exceeding 220 repeats in the 5' untranslated region of the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. Which of the following molecular epigenetic modifications is the direct mechanism by which this trinucleotide expansion causes loss of fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP) expression?

options.text: Formation of an aberrant nuclear splice-acceptor site resulting in premature nonsense codon insertion
options.explanation: Nonsense and frameshift mutations can occur in FMR1 rarely, but the overwhelming mechanism of classical CGG expansion is promoter hypermethylation and transcriptional shut-off, not aberrant splicing.

options.text: Ubiquitin-proteasome hyperactivation targeting synthesized FMRP for accelerated cytosolic degradation
options.explanation: FMRP is not synthesized and rapidly degraded; transcription of the FMR1 mRNA itself is completely shut down at the genomic promoter level by methylation.

options.text: Defective polyadenylation of the 3' untranslated region leading to rapid cytoplasmic mRNA decay
options.explanation: The CGG repeat expansion is located in the 5' untranslated region (promoter-associated), not the 3' polyadenylation signal.

options.text: Constitutive histone hyperacetylation loosening chromatin and preventing transcription factor assembly
options.explanation: Histone hyperacetylation OPENS chromatin and promotes gene transcription; in Fragile X, DNA methylation induces histone DEACETYLATION, packing chromatin into transcriptionally inert heterochromatin.

options.text: DNA hypermethylation of cytosine residues within promoter CpG islands causing transcriptional gene silencing
options.explanation: Correct. Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and the second most common genetic cause overall (after Down syndrome). It is an X-linked dominant condition caused by an unstable CGG TRINUCLEOTIDE REPEAT EXPANSION in the 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) of the FMR1 gene on the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq27.3). Normal alleles contain 5 to 44 CGG repeats; full mutation alleles contain > 200 repeats. When the repeat count exceeds 200, the massive expansion attracts DNA methyltransferases, leading to EXTENSIVE DNA HYPERMETHYLATION OF CYTOSINE BASES WITHIN CPG ISLANDS in the FMR1 promoter. This promoter hypermethylation condenses chromatin (heterochromatinization), resulting in COMPLETE TRANSCRIPTIONAL SILENCING of FMR1 and the total absence of Fragile X Mental Retardation Protein (FMRP), an essential mRNA-binding translational repressor in neurons.

subject: Genetics
topic: Friedreich Ataxia FXN GAA Repeat and Iron-Sulfur Cluster Defect
stem: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the neurology clinic because of progressive clumsiness, frequent falls, and difficulty walking that began 1 year ago. Musculoskeletal examination demonstrates severe kyphoscoliosis and high plantar arches (pes cavus). Transthoracic echocardiography reveals concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). Genetic testing reveals homozygous GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in intron 1 of the FXN gene on chromosome 9. The protein encoded by this gene (frataxin) is essential for which of the following cellular processes?

options.text: Mitochondrial iron homeostasis and biosynthesis of iron-sulfur clusters in the electron transport chain

options.explanation: Canalicular copper export is mediated by the ATP7B P-type ATPase; mutations cause Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration), not GAA-repeat ataxia with pes cavus.

options.text: Hydrolysis of very-long-chain fatty acids in peroxisomal beta-oxidation
options.explanation: Peroxisomal beta-oxidation of VLCFAs is impaired in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ABCD1 mutation) and Zellweger syndrome, not Friedreich ataxia.

topic: Huntington Disease CAG Repeat Polyglutamine and Transcriptional Repression
stem: A 42-year-old man is brought to the outpatient clinic by his wife because of progressive involuntary jerky movements of his hands and shoulders, mood irritability, and cognitive decline over the past 18 months. Physical examination reveals continuous, irregular, purposeless writhing movements of his extremities (chorea) and an unsteady, lurching gait. Mental status examination reveals impaired executive functioning and memory retrieval. His father died in a psychiatric facility at age 48 after suffering from severe dementia and choreiform movements. Brain MRI demonstrates marked bilateral atrophy of the caudate nuclei and putamen, with ex vacuo enlargement of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles. Genetic analysis confirms a heterozygous CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion (46 repeats) in the HTT gene on chromosome 4. In addition to direct toxic gain-of-function, the mutant huntingtin protein binds to and inactivates CREB-binding protein (CBP), causing which of the following downstream epigenetic alterations in striatal neurons?

options.explanation: DNA methyltransferases ADD methyl groups to cytosines (methylation), which condenses chromatin; they do not cause demethylation.

options.explanation: Correct. Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG TRINUCLEOTIDE REPEAT EXPANSION (encoding polyglutamine tracts) in the HTT gene on chromosome 4. At the molecular level, mutant huntingtin forms toxic intracellular aggregates and abnormally binds to transcription factors, including CREB-BINDING PROTEIN (CBP). CBP possesses intrinsic HISTONE ACETYLTRANSFERASE (HAT) activity. Inhibition of CBP reduces histone acetylation (causing HISTONE HYPOACETYLATION), which tightens chromatin around nucleosomes, silencing transcription of critical neuroprotective factors, including Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF).

options.text: Constitutive phosphorylation of RNA polymerase II leading to uncontrolled transcriptional elongation
options.explanation: Mutant huntingtin represses transcription of survival genes rather than stimulating uncontrolled RNA polymerase II elongation.

options.text: Impaired spliceosome assembly leading to global retention of non-coding introns in mature mRNAs
options.explanation: Huntingtin aggregates interfere primarily with transcription and vesicular transport, not global spliceosome intron excision.

options.text: Defective aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase charging of glutamine resulting in ribosome stalling and translational arrest
options.explanation: Polyglutamine tracts result from excessive CAG translation by intact glutaminyl-tRNA, not synthetase deficiency or ribosome stalling.

topic: Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1 CTG Repeat and Alternative Splicing
stem: A 32-year-old man presents with progressive muscle weakness and stiffness in his hands. He notes that after gripping a golf club or door handle, he experiences prolonged difficulty relaxing his grip and must consciously wait several seconds for his fingers to release (myotonia). Physical examination reveals bilateral temporalis and masseter muscle wasting with a long, narrow 'hatchet' facies, bilateral frontal balding, and ptosis. Direct percussion of the thenar eminence with a reflex hammer elicits prolonged sustained contraction followed by slow relaxation. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy reveals iridescent, polychromatic 'Christmas tree' cataracts in both posterior subcapsular lenses. An ECG demonstrates a prolonged PR interval (first-degree AV block). Genetic analysis reveals a CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the 3' untranslated region of the DMPK gene on chromosome 19. Which of the following molecular mechanisms directly mediates the multisystem symptoms of this condition?

options.text: Dystrophin-glycoprotein complex disruption destabilizing the sarcolemmal membrane during muscle contraction
options.explanation: Dystrophin deficiency (Duchenne/Becker) is caused by dystrophin frameshift/in-frame mutations on the X chromosome, causing proximal pseudohypertrophy, not myotonia or CTG repeats.

options.text: Immune-mediated IgG autoantibodies targeting postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
options.explanation: Antibodies against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors cause Myasthenia Gravis (fluctuating fatigable ocular/bulbar weakness), not grip myotonia or frontal balding.

options.text: Nuclear accumulation of mutant expanded CUG-repeat RNA transcripts that sequester muscleblind-like 1 (MBNL1), disrupting alternative splicing of pre-mRNAs
options.explanation: Correct. Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1 (DM1) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by an unstable CTG TRINUCLEOTIDE REPEAT EXPANSION in the 3' untranslated region (3' UTR) of the DMPK (dystrophia myotonica protein kinase) gene on chromosome 19. Normal individuals have 5-37 repeats; affected individuals have > 50 to thousands of repeats, displaying marked maternal anticipation. The mutant DMPK pre-mRNAs containing expanded CUG repeats fold into stable hairpin structures that accumulate as toxic nuclear foci. These CUG hairpins tightly bind and SEQUESTER SPLICING REGULATOR PROTEINS, notably MUSCLEBLIND-LIKE 1 (MBNL1), while upregulating CELF1. Depletion of functional MBNL1 causes widespread ABERRANT ALTERNATIVE SPLICING of developmentally regulated pre-mRNAs in multiple organs: (1) Skeletal muscle chloride channel (CLCN1) mis-splicing -> impaired membrane repolarization and myotonia; (2) Cardiac troponin T and SCN5A mis-splicing -> AV block and arrhythmias; (3) Insulin receptor (INSR) mis-splicing -> insulin resistance; (4) Lens epithelial defects -> cataracts.

options.text: Voltage-gated P/Q-type calcium channel autoantibodies impairing presynaptic acetylcholine exocytosis
options.explanation: Antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels cause Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, featuring hyporeflexia and weakness that improves with exercise, not myotonia.

options.text: Constitutive activating mutation in the skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor (RYR1) calcium release channel
options.explanation: RYR1 mutations cause Malignant Hyperthermia and Central Core Disease, triggered by volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine, not inherited CTG-repeat multisystem myotonic dystrophy.

topic: I-Cell Disease Mannose-6-Phosphate Tagging Deficiency
stem: An 8-month-old girl is evaluated for severe developmental delay, coarse facial features, and skeletal deformities. Physical examination reveals a depressed nasal bridge, prominent forehead, thick lips and gingival hyperplasia, corneal clouding, and restricted joint mobility in both shoulders and hips. Skeletal radiographs demonstrate dysostosis multiplex with anterior beaking of the lumbar vertebrae. Cultured skin fibroblasts examined under phase-contrast microscopy reveal numerous dense, refractile intracellular inclusion bodies occupying the cytoplasm. Biochemical analysis demonstrates that multiple acid hydrolase enzymes (including beta-hexosaminidase, beta-glucuronidase, and alpha-fucosidase) are virtually absent from intracellular lysosomes, but are present at 20- to 50-fold elevated concentrations in the patient's plasma and extracellular culture medium. Which of the following Golgi apparatus enzymes is primarily defective in this patient?

options.text: Lysosomal alpha-L-iduronidase in the sequential degradation of dermatan and heparan sulfate
options.explanation: Alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency causes Hurler syndrome (MPS I), which has coarse facial features and corneal clouding, but intracellular lysosomal enzyme routing is intact and plasma hydrolases are not globally elevated.

options.text: Galactosyltransferase in the assembly of core oligosaccharide chains on secretory glycoproteins
options.explanation: Galactosyltransferase mediates general N- and O-linked glycosylation in the trans-Golgi; its deficiency causes congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG), not selective loss of mannose-6-phosphate tagging.

options.text: Sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase in the conversion of sphingomyelin to ceramide and phosphocholine
options.explanation: Sphingomyelinase deficiency causes Niemann-Pick disease, characterized by hepatosplenomegaly and cherry-red spots, not global misrouting of Golgi acid hydrolases.

options.text: UDP-N-acetylglucosamine:lysosomal enzyme N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase
options.explanation: Correct. I-cell disease (mucolipidosis Type II) is a rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the Golgi enzyme UDP-N-ACETYLGLUCOSAMINE:LYSOSOMAL ENZYME N-ACETYLGLUCOSAMINYL-1-PHOSPHOTRANSFERASE (GlcNAc-phosphotransferase). In normal cell biology, acid hydrolase enzymes destined for lysosomes are synthesized in the rough ER and transported to the cis-Golgi. GlcNAc-phosphotransferase adds a phosphorylated GlcNAc to specific asparagine-linked mannose residues; a second enzyme removes the GlcNAc, leaving a MANNOSE-6-PHOSPHATE (M6P) TAG. M6P receptors in the trans-Golgi recognize this tag and package the hydrolases into clathrin-coated vesicles destined for lysosomes. In I-cell disease, absence of the phosphotransferase means acid hydrolases CANNOT BE TAGGED WITH MANNOSE-6-PHOSPHATE. Lacking the lysosomal routing signal, the enzymes are diverted by default into the constitutive secretory pathway and EXCRETED INTO THE EXTRACELLULAR SPACE AND PLASMA. Lysosomes become deficient in all hydrolases and fill with undigested substrates, forming characteristic INCLUSION BODIES ('I-cells').

options.text: Glucosylceramide beta-glucosidase in the hydrolytic cleavage of glucocerebroside
options.explanation: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease, presenting with pancytopenia and avascular bone necrosis without coarse facies, corneal clouding, or high extracellular enzyme levels.

topic: Zellweger Syndrome Peroxisomal Biogenesis Disorder
stem: A 2-day-old male newborn is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for profound generalized hypotonia, poor feeding, and recurrent focal seizures. Physical examination demonstrates severe muscular flaccidity ('floppy infant'), a flattened facial profile with a high prominent forehead, wide-open fontanelles, hypertelorism, upslanting palpebral fissures, and redundant skin folds on the neck. Abdominal ultrasound reveals bilateral cortical renal cysts and mild hepatomegaly. Brain MRI demonstrates diffuse polymicrogyria, pachygyria, and abnormal periventricular pseudocysts. Plasma biochemical profiling reveals markedly elevated concentrations of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs, including C26:0 hexacosanoic acid and C26:1), elevated phytanic acid, and severely reduced levels of plasmalogens. Cultured skin fibroblasts demonstrate an absence of functional peroxisomes due to a homozygous mutation in the PEX1 gene. Which of the following metabolic pathways is primarily dependent on the intact function of this defective organelle?

options.text: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 (CPT-1) mediated transport of long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane
options.explanation: CPT-1 resides on the outer mitochondrial membrane and initiates the carnitine shuttle for long-chain fatty acids (C14-C18) into mitochondria, not peroxisomal VLCFA processing.

options.text: Microsomal omega-oxidation of fatty acids by cytochrome P450 4A enzymes generating dicarboxylic acids
options.explanation: Omega-oxidation occurs in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (microsomes) and becomes an active alternative pathway during severe carnitine or mitochondrial beta-oxidation failure, producing dicarboxylic acids.

options.text: Mitochondrial medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) beta-oxidation generating acetyl-CoA for ketogenesis
options.explanation: MCAD resides in the mitochondrial matrix and oxidizes medium-chain fatty acids (C6-C12); MCAD deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting, without facial dysmorphism or absent peroxisomes.

options.text: Lysosomal degradation of glycosaminoglycans and sulfatides by arylsulfatase A
options.explanation: Arylsulfatase A is a lysosomal enzyme; its deficiency causes metachromatic leukodystrophy, an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease, not a peroxisome biogenesis disorder.

options.text: Initial alpha-oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids and beta-oxidation of fatty acids with chain length >= 22 carbons
options.explanation: Correct. Zellweger syndrome (cerebrohepatorenal syndrome) is the most severe PEROXISOME BIOGENESIS DISORDER (PBD), inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. It is caused by mutations in any of the PEX genes (most commonly PEX1), which encode PEROXINS—proteins essential for the import of matrix enzymes and assembly of functional peroxisomes. In the absence of peroxisomes, multiple critical biochemical pathways fail: (1) BETA-OXIDATION OF VERY-LONG-CHAIN FATTY ACIDS (VLCFAs; chain length >= 22 carbons): Peroxisomes perform the initial beta-oxidative shortening of VLCFAs down to medium-chain fatty acids, which then transfer to mitochondria for complete oxidation. (2) ALPHA-OXIDATION OF PHYTANIC ACID: Dietary branched-chain fatty acids (phytanic acid) possess a methyl group on the beta-carbon that blocks direct beta-oxidation; peroxisomal alpha-oxidation removes one carbon, generating pristanic acid for subsequent beta-oxidation (defective in Refsum disease). (3) PLASMALOGEN SYNTHESIS: Peroxisomes initiate synthesis of plasmalogens (ether phospholipids vital for myelin and heart). Accumulation of VLCFAs and phytanic acid causes severe neuronal migration defects (polymicrogyria), infantile hypotonia, facial dysmorphism, hepatomegaly, and early infant death.
